newsitem.title: KENYA: Zairean prime minister in Kenya for talks.
newsitem.headline: Zairean prime minister in Kenya for talks.

text.p: Zaire's prime minister arrived in Nairobi on Tuesday for talks on war tearing Zaire apart and said those seeking power should do so by the ballot instead of the bullet.

Ending a Zairean government boycott of two previous rounds of talks in Nairobi on the crisis in Africa's third largest country, Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo said he wished Kenya's president success in his efforts to bring peace to Zaire.
"Our presence here is an expression of the willingness of Zaire to crown with success the efforts of President Daniel arap Moi on the crisis and problems in Zaire," he told a news conference.
Asked about rebel charges that the Kinshasa government was finished and diplomats saying President Mobutu Sese Seko's rule was over, Kengo said he would not respond to rebel statements.

"Power should be taken through votes and not by violence," Kengo added. "Those who are saying they can transform Zaire should make an appointment for elections that will take place under the supervision of the international community."

A Kenyan foreign ministry spokesman said also at the talks on Wednesday would be Moi, Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe, Congolese President Pascal Lissouba, South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki and President Paul Biya of Cameroon.
But diplomats said even with Kengo the meeting would find it hard to win a push for a ceasefire and political settlement in the absence of representatives of the rebels, Rwanda and Uganda.
Laurent Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire rebels contest Kenya's role as an honest mediator, saying Moi wants to prop up his friend Mobutu.
Kenyan officials gave no dates for the subsequent regional summit -- called Nairobi Three -- but said it would be soon after Wednesday's meeting. Zaire boycotted Nairobi One and Two.

Kenya, South Africa, Zimbabwe and Cameroon were mandated by the Nairobi Two summit last December to lead African efforts to end the fighting in Zaire, where rebels have captured a fifth of its territory including the city of Kisangani at the weekend.

Since then, Kabila's forces have advanced on several fronts and are reportedly targeting mineral-rich Shaba province and Mobutu's northern jungle palace at Gbadolite near the border with the Central African Republic.
Organisation of African Unity Secretary-General Salim Ahmed Salim arrived in Nairobi on Tuesday and will join U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun at the Nairobi meeting as observers.
Salim said leaders would examine ways of ending hostilities in Zaire and pushing ahead with a political settlement.
"In any conflict it is important to first call for a cessation of hostilities. We want to examine how the hostilities could be ended and a political process started," Salim said.
Mobutu, Zaire's ruler for 32 years, was invited but is being treated for cancer in Monaco and has been in Europe most of the time since the rebels launched their revolt last October.
Zaire's government had insisted on a withdrawal of all foreign forces from east Zaire and an international monitoring force to confirm the pullout before attending Nairobi Three.
Zaire accuses Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of sending their troops to fight alongside rebels. All three deny the charges.
Analysts said the absence of South African President and Africa's elder and revered statesman Neslon Mandela was a sign he doubted the success of the Nairobi meeting without Mobutu.
Mobutu sought to rally his crumbling government against the advancing rebels on Monday by telephoning his ministers from his hospital bed in the Riviera principality of Monaco.
